# Coulomb Excitation of Low-Lying States in Unstable Nuclei at Intermediate Energies

This study investigates the Coulomb excitation of low-lying states in unstable nuclei during intermediate energy collisions, spanning a range from 10 to 500 MeV/nucleon. Understanding these excitation processes is essential for characterizing the structure and behavior of exotic nuclei that lie far from the valley of stability.

Our analysis of the excitation cross sections reveals a clear energy dependence for electromagnetic transitions. Specifically, the cross sections for both E1 (electric dipole) and E2 (electric quadrupole) transitions are found to be larger at lower collision energies. This enhancement becomes particularly pronounced well below 10 MeV/nucleon, where the interaction dynamics favor stronger coupling to these low-lying states.

An important aspect of this work concerns the physical effects that must be accounted for in an accurate theoretical treatment. We demonstrate that both retardation effects and Coulomb distortion remain relevant across the entire energy range under consideration, from 10 to 500 MeV/nucleon. This finding underscores that neither effect can be neglected when modeling intermediate energy collisions, as simplified approaches that ignore these contributions may lead to significant inaccuracies in the calculated cross sections.

These results carry important implications for experimental studies conducted at radioactive beam facilities. As such facilities continue to probe the properties of unstable nuclei, a proper accounting of retardation and Coulomb distortion effects will be crucial for the correct interpretation of Coulomb excitation data. Consequently, the findings presented here provide a valuable framework for the design and analysis of future experiments aimed at exploring the structure of nuclei far from stability.

# Coulomb Excitation of Low-Lying States in Unstable Nuclei at Intermediate Energies

## Introduction

The study of unstable nuclei has become a central focus of modern nuclear physics, driven by the development of radioactive beam facilities capable of producing and accelerating exotic isotopes far from the valley of stability. Among the most powerful experimental tools available for probing the structure of these short-lived nuclei is Coulomb excitation, a process in which the electromagnetic field generated during a collision between two nuclei induces transitions between nuclear states. Because this mechanism depends solely on the well-understood electromagnetic interaction, it provides a clean and model-independent means of extracting fundamental nuclear structure information, such as transition probabilities and multipole matrix elements.

## Scope of the Investigation

In this work, we investigate the Coulomb excitation of low-lying states in unstable nuclei during intermediate-energy collisions spanning the range of 10 to 500 MeV/nucleon. This energy regime is of particular importance because it corresponds to the conditions typically encountered at contemporary and next-generation radioactive beam facilities. Our analysis focuses on the electric dipole (E1) and electric quadrupole (E2) transition cross sections, which govern the excitation of the collective and single-particle modes most commonly studied in experiments on exotic nuclei.

A rigorous treatment of these processes requires accounting for effects that become significant when the projectile velocity approaches an appreciable fraction of the speed of light. Accordingly, we incorporate retardation effects, which arise from the finite propagation time of the electromagnetic interaction, as well as Coulomb distortion, which reflects the deviation of the projectile trajectory from a straight line due to the mutual electrostatic repulsion of the colliding nuclei. Both corrections must be handled carefully to obtain accurate predictions of the excitation cross sections.

## Principal Findings

Our calculations reveal that the transition cross sections are appreciably larger at energies well below 10 MeV/nucleon, reflecting the enhanced coupling of the nuclear system to the slowly varying electromagnetic field in this lower-energy domain. Nevertheless, we find that neither retardation nor Coulomb distortion can be safely neglected at any point within the energy range considered. Retardation effects, though most pronounced at the highest energies, remain relevant even at intermediate velocities, while Coulomb distortion continues to influence the cross sections across the entire span from 10 to 500 MeV/nucleon.

## Implications

These results carry important implications for the design and interpretation of experiments conducted at radioactive beam facilities. The simultaneous relevance of retardation and Coulomb distortion throughout the intermediate-energy regime indicates that reliable extraction of nuclear structure quantities from measured cross sections demands a consistent theoretical framework in which both effects are treated on an equal footing. By providing quantitative estimates of the E1 and E2 excitation cross sections and clarifying the conditions under which each correction becomes important, this study offers valuable guidance for optimizing experimental configurations and for improving the accuracy of nuclear structure determinations in unstable nuclei.

# The Coulomb Interaction, MeV Energy Scales, and Retardation Effects

## Introduction

In the study of electromagnetic interactions between charged particles, three interconnected concepts play crucial roles: the **Coulomb interaction**, energy measured in **MeV** (mega-electron-volts), and **retardation effects**. Together, these ideas bridge classical electromagnetism, nuclear physics, and relativistic corrections that become essential at high energies.

## The Coulomb Interaction

The Coulomb interaction describes the fundamental electrostatic force between charged particles. Named after French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, this force is described by Coulomb's law:

$$F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$$

where $q_1$ and $q_2$ are the charges, $r$ is the separation distance, and $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space. This interaction governs the attraction between electrons and nuclei in atoms, as well as the repulsion between protons in atomic nuclei. The associated potential energy determines the structure of matter across many scales.

## The MeV Energy Scale

The mega-electron-volt (MeV) represents an energy scale particularly relevant to nuclear and particle physics. One MeV equals approximately $1.602 \times 10^{-13}$ joules. At these energies, several important phenomena emerge:

- **Nuclear binding energies** typically range from a few MeV to several MeV per nucleon.
- The **Coulomb barrier** that protons must overcome to fuse in stellar cores is measured in MeV.
- **Beta and gamma decay** processes release energies in the MeV range.

At MeV energies, particle velocities can approach a significant fraction of the speed of light, making relativistic effects—including retardation—increasingly important.

## Retardation Effects

**Retardation** arises because electromagnetic influences do not propagate instantaneously but travel at the finite speed of light, $c$. When a charged particle moves, the field experienced by a distant particle reflects the source's position at an *earlier* (retarded) time, not its present position.

This leads to the concept of **retarded potentials**, which correct the simple Coulomb picture:

$$\phi(\mathbf{r}, t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \int \frac{\rho(\mathbf{r}', t_r)}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|} d^3r'$$

where $t_r = t - |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|/c$ is the retarded time.

At low velocities, retardation corrections are negligible, and the instantaneous Coulomb interaction is an excellent approximation. However, as particles reach MeV energies and relativistic speeds, these corrections become significant, giving rise to magnetic interactions and radiation effects.

## Interconnection of the Three Concepts

The interplay between these concepts is elegantly captured in the **Breit interaction**, used in relativistic atomic and nuclear physics. The Breit Hamiltonian augments the Coulomb potential with retardation and magnetic corrections:

$$H_{\text{Breit}} = \frac{e^2}{r} - \frac{e^2}{2r}\left[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_1 \cdot \boldsymbol{\alpha}_2 + \frac{(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_1 \cdot \mathbf{r})(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_2 \cdot \mathbf{r})}{r^2}\right]$$

This formulation is essential when describing electron-electron interactions in heavy atoms or nucleon interactions where energies reach the MeV scale.

## Conclusion

The Coulomb interaction, MeV energy scales, and retardation effects together illustrate the transition from classical to relativistic physics. While the static Coulomb law suffices for describing everyday electrostatics and low-energy atomic structure, the MeV domain of nuclear and high-energy physics demands careful treatment of retardation. Understanding this progression is fundamental to fields ranging from nuclear astrophysics to precision atomic spectroscopy.

# Abstract

**Coulomb Excitation of Unstable Nuclei in Intermediate-Energy Collisions**

We present a theoretical and experimental investigation of Coulomb excitation as a spectroscopic tool for studying the structure of unstable nuclei produced as radioactive ion beams. At intermediate beam energies (30–100 MeV/nucleon), the strong, time-dependent electromagnetic field generated during a peripheral collision with a high-Z target induces transitions between nuclear states, providing a nearly model-independent probe of collective properties. We develop the reaction formalism within a semiclassical framework, treating the projectile-target relative motion classically while computing excitation amplitudes through first- and higher-order perturbation theory. Particular attention is given to the extraction of reduced transition probabilities, B(E2) and B(E3) values, from measured cross sections and de-excitation γ-ray yields, including corrections for relativistic effects, nuclear contributions, and feeding from higher-lying states.

The method is applied to a series of neutron-rich isotopes, where measured 2⁺ excitation energies and transition strengths reveal the evolution of collectivity and the erosion of traditional shell closures far from stability. We demonstrate that the large excitation cross sections characteristic of intermediate energies, combined with thick-target techniques, compensate for the low intensities typical of exotic beams, enabling measurements with rates as low as a few particles per second. Systematic uncertainties associated with angular cuts, Doppler reconstruction, and the separation of Coulomb and nuclear excitation mechanisms are quantified. Our results establish intermediate-energy Coulomb excitation as a robust and sensitive technique for mapping nuclear structure across the chart of nuclides and provide benchmarks for modern shell-model and mean-field calculations of nuclei approaching the drip lines.

---

# Electric Dipole and Quadrupole Transition Cross Sections in Coulomb Excitation of Radioactive Nuclei at Intermediate Beam Energies

## Abstract

We present a comprehensive theoretical framework for calculating electric dipole (E1) and electric quadrupole (E2) transition cross sections in the Coulomb excitation of radioactive nuclear beams at intermediate energies (30–100 MeV/nucleon). At these energies, the interplay between nuclear and electromagnetic excitation mechanisms, combined with relativistic corrections and higher-order coupling effects, necessitates a careful treatment of the excitation dynamics beyond the standard first-order perturbation theory. Using a semiclassical coupled-channels approach incorporating relativistic Coulomb trajectories, we compute the energy-differential and total cross sections for both E1 and E2 excitations as functions of impact parameter, projectile charge, and excitation energy.

Our calculations demonstrate that E1 transitions dominate the excitation cross section for neutron-rich nuclei exhibiting low-lying dipole strength, particularly in the region of the pygmy dipole resonance and the soft dipole mode associated with weakly bound halo systems. In contrast, E2 excitations, while suppressed by the smaller virtual photon flux at intermediate energies, provide critical sensitivity to collective quadrupole degrees of freedom and can be selectively enhanced through appropriate choices of target and scattering angle. We quantify the relative contributions of both multipolarities and establish the kinematic conditions under which E1/E2 interference and multi-step excitation processes become non-negligible.

Particular attention is given to the extraction of reduced transition probabilities, *B*(E1) and *B*(E2), from measured cross sections, and to the systematic uncertainties introduced by nuclear diffraction, Coulomb-nuclear interference, and the choice of minimum impact parameter. We benchmark our results against experimental data for selected exotic isotopes and discuss implications for the determination of electromagnetic transition strengths in nuclei far from stability. These findings offer practical guidance for the design and interpretation of Coulomb excitation experiments at next-generation radioactive ion beam facilities.

---

*Keywords:* Coulomb excitation, radioactive ion beams, electromagnetic transition probabilities, E1 and E2 multipolarities, intermediate-energy nuclear reactions, exotic nuclei

# Abstract

Electromagnetic excitation in peripheral heavy-ion collisions has become a cornerstone technique for probing the structure of exotic nuclei at radioactive beam facilities, providing access to electric dipole strength distributions, transition probabilities, and the emergence of collective modes such as the pygmy dipole resonance. However, the accurate extraction of nuclear structure observables from measured cross sections requires careful treatment of the reaction dynamics, particularly the roles played by retardation and Coulomb distortion effects. In this article, we systematically examine how these effects modify the excitation amplitudes and virtual photon spectra across the range of beam energies characteristic of current and next-generation facilities. Retardation, arising from the finite propagation time of the electromagnetic interaction, becomes increasingly important at relativistic energies and alters the relative contributions of the electric and magnetic multipole components. Coulomb distortion, reflecting the deviation of the projectile trajectory from a straight line due to the strong nuclear Coulomb field, is shown to be significant at intermediate energies and for high-Z targets, where the point-Coulomb plane-wave approximation breaks down. Employing both semiclassical and fully quantum-mechanical coupled-channels frameworks, we quantify the deviations introduced when these effects are neglected and assess the reliability of commonly used first-order perturbation and equivalent-photon methods. Our results demonstrate that the interplay between retardation and Coulomb distortion can lead to substantial corrections in the inferred dipole response, with direct consequences for constraints on the nuclear symmetry energy and neutron skin thicknesses. We conclude by outlining the kinematic regimes in which these corrections are essential and provide practical guidance for the analysis of electromagnetic excitation experiments with weakly bound and neutron-rich systems.
